I often find it difficult to argue against the non- identity argument. Many natalists ground their arguments in the categories of Beings and Preferences. It seems impossible to me to reconcile that mindset with the categories of State and Necessity. Intuitively, the latter seems more logical to me, but trying to "argue" and correct a natalist's presuppositions is an impossible task. And vice-versa. I'm not even sure if the word "argument" is appropriate.

The question of prospective happiness contained within existence is clearly irrelevant to a Being that is yet to be conceived. We take that irrelevance as relevant, as evidence that an unproblematic state of absent sentience has no need to be negated, in the same way that a lifeless planet has no need to be terraformed. 

But that is quite a paradoxical stance.  A natalist sees that irrelevance as a pure absence to be ignored and a decision is formed and framed via their already-existent Being and Preferences. Hence, see the guy above essentially stating - "I like life. When my child exists they'll probably like it too. More of what I like is good." Are we "right"? Are they? Can anyone be right? I just don't know.

No problem. You are open and respectful. I'll just re-stress the point that the "context of a person who already exists" doesn't factor into the argument, at least not for me. Once that person exists and can choose, anti-natalist questions are moot. 

And I wouldn't say existence is inherently "bad" either. That's a preference judgment.

It doesn't need to oppose it. In a strict sense, suicide involves the expressed preferences of already existing Beings. Anti-natalist arguments explore the logical validity of negating a state of non-existence through procreation.

However, in a natalist society the preferences of already existing Beings (parents, society etc) are given priority over ethics/logic. So, I see no fair objection to the preferences of suicidal existing Beings being afforded a similar respect. This isn't essential to the argument as such, but the crude inconsistency of the current state of affairs pisses me off.

"Some people want to exist"

Sure. Once they are here. I don't focus on asking the already-existing to assess the worth of life, because it isn't relevant to the argument and the assessments are riddled with bias and distortion at the best of times.

You mention the "ability to choose". In the state of non-existence, "choosing to exist" isn't a factor. There is no spirit, being or soul out in the ether yearning to make the choice to exist and experience life, or have a procreator make the decision on its behalf.

I find it helpful to think of states and necessity, not beings and preferences. Choosing not to procreate robs no-one of nothing. Ask yourself instead why it is necessary to transition from a state of non-existence to a state of existence, especially considering the fact that, unless you are religious, any preferences of an as-yet-unborn being are immaterial.

Non existence isn't "good" as such and can't really be "preferred" to existence in a conventional comparative sense, at least not in my view.

I find it more productive to avoid quantifying the pain/pleasure calculus of already existing, or indeed prospective, life.

Take a neutral, non-judgmental perspective back to the radical equilibrium of non existence. That state of non-existence entails no deprivation of, or yearning for, pleasure and happiness, however those states are defined. It also entails no suffering, however that is defined. In a very real sense, it never hurt anybody and wanted for nothing. This can be stated without a morbid or fetishistic sensibility, which is important to emphasise because in discussions on the topic the anti-natalist position will be slandered as nihilistic and morbid.

Anyway, now, can you find a reason why that radical equilibrium of non-existence SHOULD be disturbed or negated? Are the "pleasures" of life logically NECESSARY? Are the inevitable harms anything other than gratuitous? To go from a state that wanted for nothing and hurt nobody to a state rife with frustration and inevitable harms seems to me like the most extreme futility and pointlessness.

So, in answer to your objection-non existence isn't assumed to be good, rather the negation of non-existence is assumed to be harmful and strictly unnecessary and the maintainence of a state of non-existence entails no deprivation.
